newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major refuses to prolong parliament.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major refuses to prolong parliament.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major refused on Thursday to extend parliament to allow publication of a report into sleaze charges against members of his ruling party that have soured his campaign for the May 1 election.

The Labour and Liberal Democrat opposition accused Major of trying to cover up the report into allegations that Conservative MPs were paid to ask parliamentary questions on behalf of Egyptian-born businessman Mohammed Al-Fayed.
Labour leader Tony Blair told Major: "Has this parliament not ended as it began, by a government breaking its word?"

"If he fails to have this report published when everyone knows he could, it will leave a stain on the character of his government that will only be erased by a new government with a fresh mandate that will restore confidence in our public life."

But in his last parliamentary question time before an election that polls forecast will end 18 years of Conservative rule, Major accused Labour of a "political stunt" to distract attention from excellent economic statistics.

To cheers from ranks of Conservative MPs behind him and cries of "sleaze" from Labour benches, Major shouted back: "The stain, if stain there will be, is upon a Labour front bench that have smeared and smeared and smeared again."
An interim report by a parliamentary ethics watchdog, published after pressure from the opposition, cleared 15 members of parliament on Thursday of any wrongdoing.
The 15 included Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs, who Sir Gordon Downey, parliament's commissioner for standards, said had not broken rules on declaring income from outside parliament.

But Downey said he had been unable to complete his investigation into another 10 MPs, all Conservatives, due to "the complexity of the web of accusations that have been made...and the volume of evidence produced".
Downey has been looking into the alleged payments by Al-Fayed. He has also examined payments made as election expenses to several MPs by a parliamentary lobbyist, Ian Greer.
Major declared this week that parliament must stop sitting on Friday to allow a six-week election campaign -- the longest for 80 years.

The report on the remaining 10 MPs cannot be published before the election because it has to be issued through the House of Commons standards and privileges committee, set up after earlier sleaze rows.
Labour put down a parliamentary bill on Thursday in a last-gasp bid to keep the committee sitting between Friday's closure and the official dissolution on April 8.
But it is up to the government to accept or reject the measure on Friday, and Major's clear statement that he had "no intention" of changing his plans appeared to rule that out.
His decision means the sleaze row could roll on through the election campaign, weakening hopes the ruling party may have of cutting back Labour's 25-point poll lead,
The most prominent of the 10 MPs are former ministers Neil Hamilton and Tim Smith. Smith resigned after admitting that he had failed to declare cash payments from Al-Fayed.

Hamilton has proclaimed his innocence, but in October he abandoned a libel action against the Guardian newspaper over the allegations, reviving a scandal that has dogged Major's efforts to lead his party to a record fifth election victory in a row.

The renewed focus on sleaze is likely to reinforce the hopes of Labour leader Tony Blair that he can achieve the 4.3-percent swing his party needs compared with the 1992 election to secure an overall majority in the next parliament.
